--- title: "Cohorts, Not Categories: Reading the DS Job Market Through Applicant Footprints" author: "Felix Lennert" date: "2026-03-16" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: true code-summary: "Show the code" execute: warning: false message: false freeze: true jupyter: selenium_env --- The [companion analysis](ds_jobs_mapping.html) asks an employer-side question: which job titles require similar skills? The answer is five distinct niches, each with a coherent toolset. This piece asks a purely applicant-side question, and crucially — **without using job titles at all**. Instead of grouping postings by title and then comparing the groups, we treat every individual posting as its own data point and ask: which postings attracted similar applicants? No title grouping, no normalization, no labeling. The structure — if any — has to emerge from applicant behavior alone. --- ## Data and filtering Three filters: - **≥ 20 applicants per posting** — applicant vectors below this threshold are too sparse for reliable cosine similarity - **Posted within ±14 days of at least one other posting** — removes temporally isolated postings; ensures every posting has contemporaneous neighbors so applicant pools can meaningfully overlap - **Published in 2025 or later** — the dataset spans 2013–2026, but 93 % of postings with ≥ 20 applicants are from 2025–2026. Pre-2025 postings share no applicants with current ones — different job-seeker cohorts entirely — so mixing them would produce trivial "old vs. new" clusters rather than structural signal **743 postings** survive all three filters. ::: {#54d701f3 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} pd.DataFrame({ "Stage": [ "Total postings in dataset", "After ≥ 20 applicants filter", "After temporal neighbor filter", "After 2025+ filter", "Unique applicant IDs", ], "Count": [ f"{len(df):,}", f"{len(df20):,}", f"{has_neighbor.sum():,}", f"{len(df_filt):,}", f"{len({u for lst in df_filt['applied'] for u in lst}):,}", ], }).set_index("Stage") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
Count
Stage
Total postings in dataset 3,421
After ≥ 20 applicants filter 835
After temporal neighbor filter 801
After 2025+ filter 743
Unique applicant IDs 2,276
``` ::: ::: --- ## Building the posting-level similarity matrix For each of the 743 postings we build a binary vector over the full universe of observed applicants: a 1 in position *i* means applicant *i* applied to that posting. We then compute **cosine similarity** between every pair of posting vectors. Two postings score high similarity when a large fraction of their applicants overlap — relative to their total unique applicants. Cosine normalizes for pool size, so a posting with 100 applicants and one with 30 can still score high similarity if they share most of the smaller pool. ::: {#c7b7ab3a .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} pd.DataFrame({ "Statistic": ["Min", "p25", "Median", "p75", "p90", "Max"], "Pairwise cosine similarity": [ f"{np.min(flat):.3f}", f"{np.percentile(flat, 25):.3f}", f"{np.median(flat):.3f}", f"{np.percentile(flat, 75):.3f}", f"{np.percentile(flat, 90):.3f}", f"{np.max(flat):.3f}", ], }).set_index("Statistic") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
Pairwise cosine similarity
Statistic
Min 0.000
p25 0.108
Median 0.181
p75 0.269
p90 0.361
Max 0.894
``` ::: ::: The median similarity is around 0.18. Most pairs of postings share only a small fraction of applicants — even within the DS job world, individual job seekers are not applying to every posting. --- ## Finding structure: UMAP + HDBSCAN With 743 postings and a 743 × 743 similarity matrix, we use two steps to find structure without imposing it: **UMAP** (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) reduces the high-dimensional applicant similarity structure to two dimensions. Postings that share many applicants end up close together on the map; postings with disjoint applicant pools end up far apart. **HDBSCAN** then finds density-based clusters in the 2D embedding. Unlike k-means, it does not require a pre-specified number of clusters, and it can label low-density points as noise rather than forcing them into a cluster. HDBSCAN finds **12 clusters** and marks np.int64(37) postings as noise (5% of the total). --- ## The applicant landscape ::: {#cell-fig-umap .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Build colour and label arrays for plotting colors = [color_map[c] for c in df_filt["cluster"]] labels_str = [f"Cluster {c}" if c != -1 else "Noise" for c in df_filt["cluster"]] fig = go.Figure() # Noise first (grey, behind) noise_mask = df_filt["cluster"] == -1 fig.add_trace(go.Scatter( x=df_filt.loc[noise_mask, "x"], y=df_filt.loc[noise_mask, "y"], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=5, color="#d1d5db", opacity=0.5, line=dict(width=0.5, color="white")), name="Noise", customdata=np.stack([ df_filt.loc[noise_mask, "title_raw"], df_filt.loc[noise_mask, "company"], df_filt.loc[noise_mask, "month_label"], df_filt.loc[noise_mask, "n_applied"].astype(str), ], axis=-1), hovertemplate=( "%{customdata[0]}
" "%{customdata[1]}
" "Posted: %{customdata[2]}
" "Applicants: %{customdata[3]}" ), )) # Clusters for c in cluster_ids: mask = df_filt["cluster"] == c sub = df_filt[mask] fig.add_trace(go.Scatter( x=sub["x"], y=sub["y"], mode="markers", marker=dict( size=7, color=PALETTE[cluster_ids.index(c) % len(PALETTE)], opacity=0.85, line=dict(width=0.8, color="white"), ), name=f"Cluster {c}", customdata=np.stack([ sub["title_raw"], sub["company"], sub["month_label"], sub["n_applied"].astype(str), ], axis=-1), hovertemplate=( "%{customdata[0]}
" "%{customdata[1]}
" "Posted: %{customdata[2]}
" "Applicants: %{customdata[3]}" ), )) fig.update_layout( xaxis=dict(showgrid=False, zeroline=False, showticklabels=False, title=""), yaxis=dict(showgrid=False, zeroline=False, showticklabels=False, title=""), height=580, legend=dict( orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.01, xanchor="center", x=0.5, bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.9)", bordercolor="#e5e7eb", borderwidth=1, font=dict(size=10), ), margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20), plot_bgcolor="#f9fafb", paper_bgcolor="white", font=FONT, ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-umap .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` 743 individual job postings in applicant space (UMAP). Each point is one posting — no title grouping. Proximity = shared applicants. Noise points in grey. Hover for details. ::: ::: The clusters are visible — but what drives them? Given that every posting is labeled "Data Scientist" or a close variant, the title cannot be the source of structure. Hover over individual points and look at the "Posted" field. The pattern becomes clear. --- ## What drives the clusters: time, not titles ::: {#cell-fig-date-strip .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = go.Figure() # Noise noise_mask = df_filt["cluster"] == -1 fig.add_trace(go.Box( x=df_filt.loc[noise_mask, "pub_date"].astype(np.int64) / 1e9 / 86400, name="Noise", marker_color="#d1d5db", boxpoints="all", jitter=0.4, pointpos=0, marker=dict(size=4, opacity=0.5), line=dict(width=0), fillcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", )) for c in cluster_ids: mask = df_filt["cluster"] == c fig.add_trace(go.Box( x=df_filt.loc[mask, "pub_date"].astype(np.int64) / 1e9 / 86400, name=f"Cluster {c}", marker_color=PALETTE[cluster_ids.index(c) % len(PALETTE)], boxpoints="all", jitter=0.4, pointpos=0, marker=dict(size=4, opacity=0.75), line=dict(width=1), fillcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", )) # Convert x axis (days since epoch) back to readable dates import datetime day0 = datetime.date(1970, 1, 1) ref_days = df_filt["pub_date"].astype(np.int64) / 1e9 / 86400 tick_months = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", "2026-02-01", freq="MS") tickvals = [(d - pd.Timestamp("1970-01-01")).days for d in tick_months] ticktext = [d.strftime("%b %Y") for d in tick_months] fig.update_layout( xaxis=dict( tickvals=tickvals, ticktext=ticktext, tickangle=-30, tickfont=dict(size=10), gridcolor="#f3f4f6", ), yaxis=dict(showticklabels=True, tickfont=dict(size=10)), height=420, legend=dict( orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.01, xanchor="center", x=0.5, bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.9)", bordercolor="#e5e7eb", borderwidth=1, font=dict(size=10), ), margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=60), plot_bgcolor="white", paper_bgcolor="white", font=FONT, boxmode="group", ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-date-strip .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Posting date by cluster. Each strip is one posting. Colour matches the UMAP above. The clusters stratify almost entirely by posting month — not by job title. ::: ::: The date strips reveal the structure directly. The clusters do not separate by job title — they separate by **when the posting was published**. Postings from the same month or fortnight share applicants because those job seekers were searching at the same time. A person actively browsing the market in early January 2026 leaves their fingerprint across dozens of postings published that week. The overlap of those fingerprints is what HDBSCAN picks up as a cluster. --- ## Cluster summary ::: {#98d92be2 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} rows = [] for c in cluster_ids: m = cluster_meta[c] rows.append({ "Cluster": f"Cluster {c}", "Postings": m["n"], "Date range": m["date_range"], "Median applicants": f"{m['med_app']:.0f}", "Most common state": m["top_state"], }) (pd.DataFrame(rows) .set_index("Cluster") .style.set_properties(**{"text-align": "left"}) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Some secondary patterns are visible in the cluster summaries: - **Posting volume** varies across months — some clusters are large (Cluster 0 covers the broad Jan 2025–Jan 2026 period, suggesting a persistent core cohort) while others are tight month-specific bursts - **Median applicant counts** differ across clusters — some months' postings systematically attracted more applicants per listing, possibly reflecting seasonal job-search intensity (January is historically active) - **Geographic concentration** varies: some clusters skew towards California-based remote-eligible postings, others towards Texas or nationally distributed roles --- ## What this means ### The title tells you almost nothing about who applies When we remove the title as an organizing principle, the applicant data does not spontaneously re-create title-based clusters. There is no grouping of "all Data Scientist, Fraud postings" versus "all Data Scientist, Marketing postings" — people apply to both interchangeably. The employer's taxonomy does not map onto job-seeker behavior. ### The dominant axis is time The strongest signal in applicant overlap is **posting date**. Job seekers are temporally cohorted — they enter and exit the market in waves, and each wave applies across a broad swathe of the title landscape. This means that two postings for superficially different roles, published in the same week, can share more applicants than two postings for the same role title published six months apart. ### A methodological note on title-based grouping The companion analysis groups postings by their (normalized) title and computes average skill profiles per title. This is a reasonable way to smooth out posting-level noise. But it implicitly assumes that the title is a meaningful unit of analysis — that a "Data Scientist, Marketing" posting at Company A is more similar to a "Data Scientist, Marketing" posting at Company B than to a "Data Scientist" posting at Company A. The applicant data suggests that assumption deserves scrutiny. From the job seeker's perspective, the posting — its specific company, timing, and presentation — may matter as much as its title category. ### A caveat: search result instability The entire dataset was collected by searching Hiring Cafe for "**data scientist**". This matters for interpreting the outlier clusters. Non-DS postings that appear in the dataset — "Software Engineer", "Full Stack Engineer", "Safety Data Analyst" — did so because the search engine returned them, not because they are meaningfully similar to DS roles. Search results on any platform are noisy: results shift across days as the index updates, listings are re-ranked, and adjacent roles sometimes surface. A "Software Engineer" posting landing in these results is likely an artifact of how the platform ranks listings, not a signal that software engineers and data scientists compete in the same labor market. The practical implication: **small outlier clusters that consist primarily of clearly non-DS titles should be interpreted cautiously**. Their separation from the core may reflect search result instability rather than genuine labor market segmentation. The temporal cohort finding, by contrast, operates entirely within the DS-adjacent results and is robust to this concern — the same waves of job seekers are applying to all the postings that the search returned, regardless of which ones happened to be slightly off-target. --- ## Methodology | Step | Choice | Rationale | |---|---|---| | Unit of analysis | Individual job posting (no title grouping) | Lets applicant behavior reveal structure without imposing title categories | | Applicant filter | ≥ 20 unique applicants per posting | Stable cosine similarity estimates | | Temporal filter | ≥ 1 posting within ±14 days | Removes isolated postings with no contemporaneous neighbors | | Year filter | 2025+ only | Avoids mixing incompatible applicant cohorts across years | | Similarity | Cosine on L2-normalized binary applicant vectors | Normalizes for pool size | | Dimensionality reduction | UMAP (cosine metric, n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.2) | Preserves local similarity structure in 2D | | Clustering | HDBSCAN (min_cluster_size=12, min_samples=3) | Density-based; no k required; handles noise |
